claims.claim: Calb2 expression is found in PVT1P and PVT5pan.
claims.source: Here, we find that Calb2 expression is found in PVT1P and PVT5pan, which is consistent with previous reports that expression of this gene is found across the PVT (Mátyás et al., 2018; Hua et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the gene expression data shown in Figure 4d and is consistent with previous reports.

claims.claim: All five PVT subtypes lacked Pvalb expression.
claims.source: Consistent with descriptions of the PVT as a higher-order midline thalamic structure, all five PVT subtypes lacked Pvalb expression (Figure 4d; Jones and Hendry, 1989; Jones, 2001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the gene expression data shown in Figure 4d and is consistent with the classification of PVT as a higher-order thalamic nucleus.

claims.claim: Calb1 expression was only found in PVT2edge and PVT5pan subtypes, with higher expression in PVT2edge.
claims.source: Notably, Calb1 expression was only found in PVT2edge and PVT5pan subtypes, with higher expression in PVT2edge.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the gene expression data shown in Figure 4d.

claims.claim: The core and matrix dichotomy is not a sufficient classification system to encompass all thalamic cell types.
claims.source: This result alongside other studies lends support to the notion that the core and matrix dichotomy is not a sufficient classification system to encompass all thalamic cell types (Phillips et al., 2019; Clascá et al., 2012; Halassa and Sherman, 2019).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on the gene expression data and previous literature.

claims.claim: The midline-thalamic dataset and the ThalamoSeq dataset contained mostly non-overlapping transcriptomes.
claims.source: Upon clustering analysis and plotting the UMAP of the integrated dataset with all midline-thalamic and BSTpr neurons, we found that our midline-thalamic dataset and the ThalamoSeq dataset contained mostly non-overlapping transcriptomes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the integration analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The clusters representing PVT1P and PVT2edge contained overlap with PFC-projectors.
claims.source: Following this, comparing the proportion of cortical-projectors in the integrated dataset showed that the clusters representing PVT1P and PVT2edge contained overlap with PFC-projectors, whereas, unexpectedly, the cluster representing PVT4AM had a small amount of overlap with auditory and visual projectors (Figure 5b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the integration analysis shown in Figure 5b.

claims.claim: The cluster representing PVT4AM had a small amount of overlap with auditory and visual projectors.
claims.source: Following this, comparing the proportion of cortical-projectors in the integrated dataset showed that the clusters representing PVT1P and PVT2edge contained overlap with PFC-projectors, whereas, unexpectedly, the cluster representing PVT4AM had a small amount of overlap with auditory and visual projectors (Figure 5b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the integration analysis shown in Figure 5b.

claims.claim: Col12a1 is a conserved marker across PFC-projectors and PVT2edge cells.
claims.source: Next, we performed conserved marker analysis across these five integrated clusters and confirmed that Col12a1 is a conserved marker across PFC-projectors and PVT2edge cells (Figure 5f, Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the conserved marker analysis shown in Figure 5f.

claims.claim: The Col12a1-positive PVT2edge subtype represents a subpopulation of neurons that project to the PFC.
claims.source: These findings suggest that the Col12a1-positive PVT2edge subtype represents a subpopulation of neurons that project to the PFC, which is consistent with prior studies indicating that pPVT neurons are anatomically linked to the prelimbic cortex (PL) in a cortico-thalamocortical loop (Gao et al., 2020; Li and Kirouac, 2008; Moga et al., 1995; Li and Kirouac, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on the integration analysis and is consistent with previous anatomical studies.

claims.claim: The majority of retrobeads-labeled cells from PL injections resided in the ventral edge of the PVT and partially co-localized with Col12a1-expressing cells.
claims.source: Consistent with the RPCA analysis, the results of this experiment revealed that the majority of retrobeads-labeled cells resided in the ventral edge of the PVT and partially co-localized with Col12a1-expressing cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the retrograde tracing and ISH data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: PVT efferent and afferent connectivity with the PL is restricted to the ventral edge of the pPVT.
claims.source: Also, in agreement with our results, anatomical tracing studies from the Mouse Connectome Project revealed that PVT efferent and afferent connectivity with the PL is restricted to the ventral edge of the pPVT (Figure 5—figure supplement 3, https://www.mouseconnectome.org/; Zingg et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data from the Mouse Connectome Project shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Anterior-biased thalamic regions including the aPVT (but not the pPVT) send projections to known auditory and visual cortical areas, such as the temporal association cortex.
claims.source: Consistent with the results from our comparative analysis with the ThalamoSeq dataset, this search revealed four experiments demonstrating that anterior-biased thalamic regions including the aPVT (but not the pPVT) send projections to known auditory and visual cortical areas, such as the temporal association cortex (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data from the Allen Brain Mouse Connectivity Atlas shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: Different PVT subtypes, namely PVT1P, PVT2edge, and PVT4AM, share conserved markers with different thalamo-cortical projectors.
claims.source: Collectively, the integrative analysis performed here supports that different PVT subtypes, namely PVT1P, PVT2edge, and PVT4AM, share conserved markers with different thalamo-cortical projectors.
claims.evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the integration analysis with the ThalamoSeq dataset.

claims.claim: Functionally distinct thalamic domains are organized in continuous neuronal gradients.
claims.source: Recently, our group and others have demonstrated that, contrary to the traditional discrete parcellations of thalamic nuclei, functionally distinct thalamic domains are organized in continuous neuronal gradients.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of recent findings from the authors' group and others.

claims.claim: The PVT, TRN, and MD thalamus have each been shown to contain at least two genetically defined cell types that are organized in opposing spatial gradients and reflect distinct anatomical connectivity, electrophysiological signatures, and functional contributions.
claims.source: Specifically, the PVT, TRN, and MD thalamus have each been shown to contain at least two genetically defined cell types that are organized in opposing spatial gradients and reflect distinct anatomical connectivity, electrophysiological signatures, and functional contributions (Gao et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020; Mukherjee et al., 2021; Martinez-Garcia et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: PVT subtypes are organized in a combination of topographical gradients (e.g. medio-lateral, antero-posterior, dorso-ventral), which has not yet been reported in another midline thalamic area.
claims.source: Importantly, these PVT subtypes are organized in a combination of topographical gradients (e.g. medio-lateral, antero-posterior, dorso-ventral), which, to our knowledge, has not yet been reported in another midline thalamic area.
claims.evidence: This is a novel finding from the spatial mapping data.

claims.claim: This feature of multiple gradients is likely conserved and may serve as a basis for new conceptual models across the midline and intralaminar thalamic organization.
claims.source: However, given that thalamic pathways consist of repeated molecular architectures (Phillips et al., 2019), it is likely that this feature of multiple gradients is conserved and may serve as a basis for new conceptual models across the midline and intralaminar thalamic organization.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the findings and previous literature.

claims.claim: The four subtypes can be split into two major branches: (1) PVT1P, PVT2edge and (2) PVT3AL, PVT4AM.
claims.source: From our molecular and spatial mapping, we found that the four subtypes can be split into two major branches: (1) PVT1P, PVT2edge and (2) PVT3AL, PVT4AM.
claims.evidence: This is based on the phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2b.

claims.claim: One major axis of separation between the two branches lies in their rostral-caudal distribution.
claims.source: These two branches consist of the posterior-biased, and anterior-biased subtypes, respectively, indicating that one major axis of separation between these two branches lies in their rostral-caudal distribution.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the spatial distribution data.

claims.claim: Markers from the same cluster had a similar spatial distribution but labeled portions of non-overlapping neurons.
claims.source: Notably, when selecting a second set of markers to label either anterior-biased or posterior-biased subtypes, we found that markers from the same cluster had a similar spatial distribution but labeled portions of non-overlapping neurons.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the multiplex ISH data shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claims.claim: PVT neurons express unique intrinsic properties that undergo diurnal fluctuations associated with changes in gene expression.
claims.source: There is a formative body of evidence supporting that PVT neurons express unique intrinsic properties that undergo diurnal fluctuations associated with changes in gene expression (Kolaj et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: PVT neuronal firing properties are affected by a variety of neuromodulators, which may contribute to differences in their electrophysiological signatures.
claims.source: PVT neuronal firing properties are also documented to be affected by a variety of neuromodulators, which may contribute to differences in their electrophysiological signatures (Kolaj et al., 2012; Kolaj et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous electrophysiological studies.

claims.claim: Neuromodulator influence in the PVT is higher than other neighboring thalamic regions, perhaps owing to its selective innervation by the hypothalamus and brainstem.
claims.source: Additionally, neuromodulator influence in the PVT is higher than other neighboring thalamic regions, perhaps owing to its selective innervation by the hypothalamus and brainstem (Kirouac, 2015; Krout and Loewy, 2000b; Krout et al., 2002; Vertes, 1991; Krout and Loewy, 2000a).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claims.claim: The previously reported effects of neuromodulators on the intrinsic properties of PVT neurons are likely to be diverse across subtypes.
claims.source: Given that each subtype contains the differential expression of neuromodulator receptor systems and ion channels, the previously reported effects of neuromodulators on the intrinsic properties of PVT neurons are likely to be diverse across subtypes (Chen et al., 2015; Kolaj et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2013; Kolaj et al., 2007; Ishibashi et al., 2005; Ong et al., 2017; Heilbronner et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the differential gene expression data and previous literature.

claims.claim: There is growing interest in the human PVT as a putative target for affective and substance abuse disorders.
claims.source: Indeed, based on the role of the rodent PVT in emotional processing and motivated behaviors, there is growing interest in the human PVT as a putative target for affective and substance abuse disorders, particularly since the human PVT has similar connectivity with the rodent PVT (Kark et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recent review.

claims.claim: The existence of some markers (e.g. Drd2, Drd3) reported in the present atlas has been corroborated in the human PVT.
claims.source: Excitingly, the existence of some markers (e.g. Drd2, Drd3) reported in our present atlas has already been corroborated in the human PVT, supporting that our atlas may provide conserved gene markers across species (Rieck et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on the human PVT.

claims.claim: The pPVT selectively innervates PL, nucleus accumbens core and ventromedial shell, central and basolateral amygdala, and lateral BST.
claims.source: From classical tracing studies, the pPVT selectively innervates PL, nucleus accumbens core and ventromedial shell, central and basolateral amygdala, and lateral BST (Li and Kirouac, 2008; Moga et al., 1995).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to classical anatomical tracing studies.

claims.claim: PVT2edge cells belong to a group of Col12a1-expressing PFC-projectors that reside on the ventroposterior edge of the PVT.
claims.source: Of note, our integrative analysis with the ThalamoSeq atlas showed that PVT2edge cells in particular belong to a group of Col12a1-expressing PFC-projectors that reside on the ventroposterior edge of the PVT (Phillips et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the integration analysis shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Prelimbic afferents to the pPVT are spatially distributed in a manner that resembles the ventroposterior location of PVT2edge cells.
claims.source: Intriguingly, anterograde viral tracing from multiple studies reveals that prelimbic afferents to the pPVT are spatially distributed in a manner that resembles the ventroposterior location of PVT2edge cells, lending support to the idea that PVT2edge cells may be preferentially integrated into a cortico-thalamocortical pathway that mediates its role in cognitive processes related to emotional and motivational states (Figure 5—figure supplement 2; Zingg et al., 2014; Campus et al., 2019; Otis et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data from the Mouse Connectome Project and other studies.

claims.claim: PVT2edge cells may be preferentially integrated into a cortico-thalamocortical pathway that mediates its role in cognitive processes related to emotional and motivational states.
claims.source: Intriguingly, anterograde viral tracing from multiple studies reveals that prelimbic afferents to the pPVT are spatially distributed in a manner that resembles the ventroposterior location of PVT2edge cells, lending support to the idea that PVT2edge cells may be preferentially integrated into a cortico-thalamocortical pathway that mediates its role in cognitive processes related to emotional and motivational states (Figure 5—figure supplement 2; Zingg et al., 2014; Campus et al., 2019; Otis et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on anatomical data and previous functional studies.

claims.claim: Prefrontal projections to the PVT guide the expression of emotional memory-associated behaviors such as conditioned fear and cue-reward food seeking.
claims.source: Indeed, prefrontal projections to the PVT guide the expression of emotional memory-associated behaviors such as conditioned fear and cue-reward food seeking (Campus et al., 2019; Otis et al., 2019; Do-Monte et al., 2015; Quiñones-Laracuente et al., 2021; Otis et al., 2017; Haight and Flagel, 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to functional studies.

claims.claim: PVT1P neurons specifically express Esr1 (estrogen receptor 1), a cell marker for ventromedial hypothalamic (VMH) neurons that control aggression and mating.
claims.source: Additionally, PVT1P neurons specifically express Esr1 (estrogen receptor 1), a cell marker for ventromedial hypothalamic (VMH) neurons that control aggression and mating, which are stereotyped and conserved behaviors under the control of subcortical networks (Lee et al., 2014; Hashikawa et al., 2017; Falkner and Lin, 2014; Liu et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the gene expression data and citations to studies on VMH function.

claims.claim: The PVT receives heavy afferents from Esr1-expressing VMH neurons.
claims.source: Whether Esr1 neurons in the PVT contribute to the control of aggressive and mating behavior is not known; however, the PVT receives heavy afferents from Esr1-expressing VMH neurons, anatomically linking these two structures and prompting further investigation (Lo et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an anatomical study.

claims.claim: PVT2edge may consist of a genetic subpopulation that is preferentially involved in aspects of behavior requiring cortical processing.
claims.source: Altogether, we propose that PVT2edge may consist of a genetic subpopulation that is preferentially involved in aspects of behavior requiring cortical processing, whereas the PVT1P subtype may contain neurons differentially recruited by tasks involving subcortical or cortical networks depending on their location.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the anatomical and gene expression data.

claims.claim: The PVT1P subtype may contain neurons differentially recruited by tasks involving subcortical or cortical networks depending on their location.
claims.source: Altogether, we propose that PVT2edge may consist of a genetic subpopulation that is preferentially involved in aspects of behavior requiring cortical processing, whereas the PVT1P subtype may contain neurons differentially recruited by tasks involving subcortical or cortical networks depending on their location.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the anatomical and gene expression data.

claims.claim: Some neurons within PVT4AM may send anatomical projections to auditory and visual cortical areas.
claims.source: One surprising observation generated by the RPCA-based integration of our dataset with the ThalamoSeq atlas is the notion that some neurons within PVT4AM may send anatomical projections to auditory and visual cortical areas (Figure 5c and f).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the integration analysis shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: The aPVT projects to auditory and visual areas that have been implicated in or suggested to regulate limbic functions.
claims.source: This assertion is further supported by anterograde tracing studies showing that the aPVT projects to auditory and visual areas that have been implicated in or suggested to regulate limbic functions (Figure 5—figure supplement 4; Dalmay et al., 2019; Cho et al., 2016; Yu et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data from the Allen Brain Atlas and citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The PVT4AM participates in modulating emotional responses to salient stimuli in part through its interaction with limbic cortical areas beyond the PFC.
claims.source: Given the PVT's role in emotional salience processing, these findings raise the possibility that the PVT4AM participates in modulating emotional responses to salient stimuli in part through its interaction with limbic cortical areas beyond the PFC (Gao et al., 2020; Haight et al., 2017; Zhu et al., 2018; Garau et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the connectivity data and previous functional studies.

claims.claim: This study provides the first comprehensive molecular and spatial profiling of cell types across the entirety of the PVT.
claims.source: In conclusion, while there have been some investigations into the molecular organization of the PVT, here we have provided the first comprehensive molecular and spatial profiling of cell types across the entirety of the PVT (Phillips et al., 2019; Gaspari et al., 2022; Nagalski et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is a claim about the novelty and comprehensiveness of the study.

claims.claim: The PVT is a critical integrative node linking circuits of internal and external processing with those involved in arousal signaling, as well as instrumental and Pavlovian behavioral control.
claims.source: The PVT is a critical integrative node linking circuits of internal and external processing with those involved in arousal signaling, as well as instrumental and Pavlovian behavioral control (Kirouac, 2021; McNally, 2021; Penzo and Gao, 2021; Kelley et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent reviews.

claims.claim: The discovery of five spatially segregated PVT neuronal subtypes should serve as a basis for resolving previously conflicting observations.
claims.source: Our discovery of five spatially segregated PVT neuronal subtypes should serve as a basis for resolving previously conflicting observations and offer a starting point for new mechanistic inquiries as to how PVT offers control over its diverse range of functional correlates.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement about the implications of the findings.

claims.claim: Tissue punches from the entire antero-posterior PVT from four P90 adult C57BL/6 J mice were collected and pooled together for each individual sample.
claims.source: Tissue punches from the entire antero-posterior PVT from four P90 adult C57BL/6 J mice (12 weeks) were dissected and pooled together for each individual sample and a total of four biological replicates were collected.
claims.evidence: This describes the sample collection method used in the study.

claims.claim: Nuclei were obtained using the mechanical-detergent lysis protocol described in Matson et al., 2018.
claims.source: Nuclei were obtained using the mechanical-detergent lysis protocol described step-by-step in Matson et al., 2018.
claims.evidence: This describes the nuclei isolation method used in the study.

claims.claim: Samples were sequenced using the Illumina, Inc NovaSeq 6000 system.
claims.source: Samples were sequenced using the Illumina, Inc NovaSeq 6000 system to yield a single nuclei dataset.
claims.evidence: This describes the sequencing platform used in the study.

claims.claim: Integration using the Harmony algorithm was implemented to minimize experimental batch effects.
claims.source: Next, low-quality nuclei and doublets were removed based on standard criteria (i.e. level of mitochondrial transcripts, number of genes), and integration using the Harmony algorithm was implemented to minimize experimental batch effects (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Korsunsky et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This describes the computational method used to correct for batch effects.

claims.claim: Cells were considered positive for a given gene if they contained a minimum of seven mRNA transcripts (dots).
claims.source: This pipeline was modified to include up to 12 mRNA probes and cells were considered positive for a given gene if they contained a minimum of seven mRNA transcripts (dots).
claims.evidence: This describes the threshold used for calling positive cells in the ISH analysis.

results.result: Single-nucleus RNA sequencing of PVT tissue identified 16 clusters from 20,503 nuclei, which were classified into 7 major cell types including neurons. PVT neurons (5,737 nuclei, 58.3% of all neurons) were identified based on marker expression, along with neurons from adjacent regions (MD, IMD, BSTpr, Hb).
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C23-C30 are well-supported by the clustering analysis, marker gene expression data (Figure 1), and validation with Allen Brain Atlas ISH data. The methods describe appropriate quality control, batch correction using Harmony, and standard clustering approaches. The identification of cell types using canonical markers is consistent with established practices.

results.result: Five molecularly distinct PVT neuronal subtypes (PVT1-5) were identified through clustering analysis. PVT1, PVT2, and PVT5 formed one major branch, while PVT3 and PVT4 formed another. Only PVT1 expressed Drd2, refining the previous binary classification of PVT neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C34 are supported by the clustering data (Figure 2a), phylogenetic analysis (Figure 2b), and differential gene expression analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1). The identification of five subtypes rather than two represents a refinement of previous work and is well-documented with appropriate statistical methods.

results.result: Multiplex fluorescent in situ hybridization revealed that PVT subtypes are organized along multiple spatial gradients: antero-posterior, medio-lateral, and dorso-ventral. PVT1/Esr1 and PVT2/Col12a1 are posterior-biased, PVT3/Npffr1 and PVT4/Hcrtr1 are anterior-biased with medio-lateral segregation, and PVT5/Drd3 is distributed pan-PVT.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C20, C35-C37, C40-C43, C48 are strongly supported by the multiplex ISH data (Figure 3) with quantitative analysis showing statistically significant differences in spatial distribution (p<0.0001 for anterior vs. posterior comparisons). The spatial mapping validates the sequencing results and demonstrates novel organizational features.

results.result: A second set of markers (Drd2, Pde3a, Insrr, Npsr1) showed similar spatial distribution to the initial markers but with only 30% or less overlap at the single-cell level, indicating high gene expression diversity within PVT subtypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C47, C82 are supported by the multiplex ISH validation data (Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3). The observation of limited overlap between markers from the same cluster is well-documented, though the functional implications remain speculative (C47). The data quality and quantification methods appear appropriate.

results.result: Hierarchical clustering based on spatial ISH data suggested PVT3 and PVT4 are more closely related to PVT5 than to PVT1 and PVT2, differing from the sequencing-based phylogenetic tree due to differences in distance matrix calculation methods.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C39 acknowledge a discrepancy between spatial and sequencing-based clustering and provide a reasonable methodological explanation. The authors appropriately note that spatial data uses one marker per cluster while sequencing uses all genes, providing complementary information. This transparent reporting of methodological differences is appropriate.

results.result: The five PVT subtypes show differential expression of neuromodulatory receptors and ion channels. Examples include Npffr1 in PVT3AL, Ldlr in PVT1, differential dopamine receptor expression (Drd1 in PVT3AL, Drd3 in PVT5pan, Drd2 in PVT1P), and subtype-specific expression of T-type calcium channels and potassium channels.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C57, C59-C61 are supported by the gene expression data shown in Figure 4. The differential expression patterns are clearly documented and provide molecular insights into potential functional differences. The data presentation is appropriate with both percent expression and average expression levels shown.

results.result: Analysis of calcium-binding protein expression revealed that Calb2 is expressed in PVT1P and PVT5pan, all PVT subtypes lack Pvalb, and Calb1 is only found in PVT2edge and PVT5pan. This pattern challenges the traditional core/matrix dichotomy for thalamic classification.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C66 are supported by the gene expression data (Figure 4d) and are consistent with the PVT's classification as a higher-order thalamic nucleus. The interpretation regarding the core/matrix dichotomy (C66) is appropriately supported by citations to previous work and represents a valid inference from the data.

results.result: RPCA-based integration with the ThalamoSeq atlas revealed that PVT subtypes differentially innervate cortical areas. PVT1P and PVT2edge overlap with PFC-projectors (with Col12a1 as a conserved marker for PVT2edge), while PVT4AM shows unexpected overlap with auditory and visual cortical projectors.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C21, C67-C71, C75 are supported by the integration analysis (Figure 5) and conserved marker analysis. The finding of PVT4AM overlap with auditory/visual projectors is noted as unexpected but is validated by Allen Brain Atlas connectivity data (Figure 5—figure supplement 4). The integration methodology using RPCA is appropriate and well-described.

results.result: Retrograde tracing from prelimbic cortex (PL) confirmed that PL-projecting neurons reside in the ventral edge of the pPVT and partially co-localize with Col12a1-expressing cells, consistent with the integration analysis and Mouse Connectome Project data.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C73 are supported by the retrograde tracing experiment (Figure 5—figure supplement 2) and Mouse Connectome Project data (Figure 5—figure supplement 3). This provides independent validation of the computational integration results. However, the sample size is small (N=2) for the retrograde tracing experiment.

results.result: Anterior-biased thalamic regions including aPVT send projections to auditory and visual cortical areas such as the temporal association cortex, as revealed by Allen Brain Atlas connectivity data and supported by the integration analysis showing PVT4AM overlap with auditory/visual projectors.
results.evaluation: Claims C74, C98-C99 are supported by Allen Brain Atlas connectivity data (Figure 5—figure supplement 4) and the integration analysis (Figure 5). The convergence of computational integration results with anatomical tracing data strengthens these findings. However, the functional significance remains to be determined.

results.result: The dataset contains largely non-overlapping transcriptomic profiles compared to the ThalamoSeq dataset and includes complementary, previously unexplored mouse thalamic single-nuclei transcriptomes from MD and IMD.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C22 are supported by the integration analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) showing minimal overlap between datasets. The identification of MD and IMD neurons is supported by marker gene expression and Allen Brain Atlas validation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2). This represents a valuable resource for the field.

results.result: PVT subtypes are organized in a combination of topographical gradients (medio-lateral, antero-posterior, dorso-ventral), which has not been reported in another midline thalamic area. The four spatially-biased subtypes split into two branches: posterior-biased (PVT1P, PVT2edge) and anterior-biased (PVT3AL, PVT4AM).
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C81 are supported by the spatial mapping data (Figure 3) and phylogenetic analysis (Figure 2b). The novelty claim (C78) is appropriately qualified with 'to our knowledge.' The speculation about conservation across thalamic regions (C79) is reasonable but remains to be tested.

results.result: Differential expression of voltage-gated potassium channels and neuromodulator receptors may underlie variability in membrane properties and neuromodulator effects across PVT subtypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C62, C86 are speculative interpretations based on gene expression data and previous literature. While the differential expression is well-documented, the functional implications require electrophysiological validation. The claims are appropriately presented as possibilities ('may underlie,' 'likely to be diverse') but lack direct experimental support.

results.result: The authors propose that PVT2edge may be preferentially involved in cortical processing-dependent behaviors, PVT1P may be recruited by tasks involving subcortical or cortical networks depending on location, and PVT4AM may modulate emotional responses through interactions with limbic cortical areas beyond PFC.
results.evaluation: Claims C92, C96-C97, C100 are speculative proposals based on anatomical connectivity and gene expression data. While the anatomical evidence is solid, the functional claims require behavioral and physiological validation. The authors appropriately present these as proposals and possibilities, but they remain hypotheses to be tested.

results.result: This study provides the first comprehensive molecular and spatial profiling of cell types across the entirety of the PVT, which should serve as a basis for resolving previously conflicting observations.
results.evaluation: Claims C101, C103 are supported by the comprehensive nature of the dataset and appropriate citations to previous work. The claim of being 'first comprehensive' is justified given the scope of the snRNA-seq and spatial mapping. The potential impact on resolving conflicting observations is a reasonable expectation based on the identification of five spatially segregated subtypes.

results.result: The study used tissue punches from four P90 C57BL/6J mice, nuclei isolation using mechanical-detergent lysis, sequencing on Illumina NovaSeq 6000, Harmony algorithm for batch correction, and a threshold of seven mRNA transcripts for positive cell calling in ISH.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C108 describe the methodological approaches used in the study. These are well-documented in the Methods section with appropriate citations. The sample size (N=4 biological replicates for sequencing, N=3 for ISH) is reasonable for this type of study. The threshold of 7 transcripts for ISH is clearly stated but lacks justification.

results.result: The introduction establishes that PVT regulates diverse cognitive and behavioral processes, shows functional heterogeneity that has yielded conflicting results, and that molecular identity can delineate functionally distinct cell types, motivating the need for systematic transcriptional profiling.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C7-C19 provide background context supported by extensive citations to previous literature. These claims appropriately frame the knowledge gap (C2, C16) and rationale (C19) for the study. The citations appear appropriate and the summary of prior work is accurate based on the references provided.

results.result: The discussion contextualizes findings within prior work on thalamic organization, neuromodulation, connectivity, and translational relevance to human PVT, supported by extensive citations to previous literature.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C52, C58, C76-C77, C83-C85, C87-C89, C93-C95, C102 provide appropriate context from previous literature to interpret the current findings. The citations appear accurate and relevant. The discussion of translational relevance (C87-C88) is appropriately cautious and supported by citations.
